opus-5.5.text:
I think there's actually a lot of room, and it's easy to miss because the headlines are dominated by the big labs training giant foundation models. But a frontier model on its own doesn't put a robot to work in a warehouse or a hospital or on a farm. There's a huge gap between a model that can do impressive things in a demo and a system that does something reliably, thousands of times a day, in a specific messy environment, at a cost that makes economic sense.

So I'd think of it in layers. At the bottom you have the foundation model builders, and yes, that takes enormous compute and data, so it'll mostly be big tech and a handful of very well-funded startups. But above that there's a lot to do. There's hardware: we still need cheaper, more robust arms, hands, grippers and sensors, and the models are only as good as the bodies they control. There's data, because robotics doesn't have an internet's worth of free training data. Companies that can collect high-quality, diverse demonstration data, whether through teleoperation, simulation, or deployed fleets, will have something really valuable.

Then there's the application layer, which I think is the most underrated. If you deeply understand a vertical, say food handling, lab automation, or construction, you know the edge cases, the safety requirements, and the workflows. You can take a general model and fine-tune it, wrap it with the right guardrails and the right evaluation, and actually deliver value to a customer. Big tech generally doesn't want to go door to door integrating into a thousand different factories. That's where smaller companies win.

And finally there's infrastructure and tooling: evaluation, safety monitoring, fleet management, simulation, deployment pipelines. As these models become more general, someone has to figure out how you know a robot is safe enough to put next to people, and how you debug it when it fails.

So my view is that the frontier models are more like a platform shift. They lower the barrier to building capable robots, much like cloud computing lowered the barrier to building software companies. The value doesn't all accrue to whoever builds the platform. A lot of it goes to whoever figures out how to make it useful in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says there is “a lot of room” beyond big tech and explains that smaller companies can succeed in hardware, data, applications, and infrastructure as frontier models advance.

r002.rationale: It says value does not all accrue to the platform builder and describes companies using a general model to deliver useful products in specific industries.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because I actually think the opportunity is bigger than people assume, even if the shape of it is different from what we've seen in software.

Let me start with what's true. Training a frontier model, the kind of thing that gives a robot general visual and language understanding, takes capital and compute that only a handful of organizations have. So if you're a startup or a mid-sized industrial company, you are probably not going to pretrain your own foundation model from scratch. I don't think that's a tragedy, though. It's the same situation every company that builds on cloud infrastructure or on a large language model API is in today.

Where it gets interesting is that robotics is not just a model problem. There's the physical hardware, the actuators, the sensors, the integration into a real workflow. There's the data from the actual environment where the robot has to operate, which is a warehouse, a hospital, a kitchen, a farm. And there's the last mile of reliability, which in robotics is brutal. Getting from a demo that works eighty percent of the time to a product that works ninety-nine point nine percent of the time is where most of the value gets created and most of the engineering happens. Big tech is not well positioned to do that for every vertical. They don't have the domain knowledge, the customer relationships, or frankly the patience for each niche.

So the way I'd frame it, the frontier models become something like a commodity layer, maybe a very valuable commodity, but still a layer you build on top of. And the companies that win are the ones who own a specific embodiment, a specific task domain, and the proprietary data that comes from actually deploying robots in the world. That data flywheel is a real moat. If you've got a hundred robots running in food processing facilities collecting failure cases every day, a foundation model lab can't easily replicate that, and the model providers want that data as much as you want their model.

The other thing I'd say is that post-training is becoming accessible in a way pretraining never will be. Fine-tuning a vision-language-action model on your own task distribution, with a modest amount of teleoperation or demonstration data, is something a small team can do now. That's the open opportunity. It shifts the question from who has the biggest cluster to who understands the problem best and can collect the right data fast.

I'd also point out that open-weight models change the calculus. If a strong open model exists, the pricing power of the frontier labs over robotics companies is limited, and a lot of the differentiation moves to hardware and deployment. I'm fairly optimistic there will be good open options in this space, partly because the robotics research community has a strong culture of releasing models and datasets.

If I'm being honest about the risks, the one that worries me is if the frontier labs decide to go vertical themselves, build the hardware, own the deployment. That's possible. But the history of technology suggests that platform companies rarely do a good job in every vertical, and the surface area of the physical world is enormous. There's a lot of room.

r001.rationale: The response describes broad opportunities and accessible post-training, but does not clearly state that rapid AI innovation creates room for many companies to succeed.

r002.rationale: It says companies can build on foundation models supplied by others and create value through their own hardware, workflow integration, deployment data, and reliability.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of opportunity, because a frontier model is only one part of a robotics system. You still have to make that system useful and reliable in a particular environment, and that requires hardware, data, integration, and a really good understanding of the customer’s problem.

For a smaller company, the question is: What task can you solve well, and what access do you have that others don’t? Maybe you have a close relationship with customers in a particular industry. You can deploy robots, understand where they fail, and collect data that helps you improve the system. That can be a very valuable advantage, even if you aren’t training the underlying model from scratch.

There’s a dependency there, of course. How accessible these models are, how much they cost, and how much you can adapt them will matter. But if general capabilities become easier to access, that could let more companies focus on the application. The opportunity is to take those capabilities and turn them into something that consistently does useful work.

r001.rationale: The response describes opportunities for smaller companies if general capabilities become easier to access, but does not state that rapid AI innovation creates room for many companies to succeed.

r002.rationale: It says smaller companies can create value by applying accessible models to specific tasks, even if they do not train the underlying model themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of opportunity, because a frontier model is only one piece of a robotics system. You still have to figure out what the robot should do, collect data in the environment where it’s going to operate, build the hardware, and make the whole system reliable enough that someone will pay for it.

A company that deeply understands a particular application can have a real advantage. What are the tasks that matter to the customer? What does success look like? How do you recover when something goes wrong? Those questions are very specific to the deployment, and a general model doesn’t automatically answer them.

The interesting question is how much you can build on top of models that are available to everyone, and where you need your own capabilities. If you can use a frontier model as a starting point, then your deployment experience and the data you collect can become a feedback loop for improving the product. So I don’t think every robotics company needs to train a frontier model from scratch. There’s room to build valuable companies around getting robots to do useful work consistently.

r001.rationale: The response says there is substantial opportunity in robotics, but it does not connect that opportunity to rapid innovation in AI.

r002.rationale: The response says companies can use frontier models available to everyone as a starting point and build valuable robotics businesses through deployment expertise and data, without training their own model from scratch.
